title: SoFi Faces Valuation Headwinds as Competitors Validate Its Bank Charter Strategy
subtitle: Chime put a $590 million price tag on owning a charter, but shrinking software fees keep SoFi priced like a lender.
summary: Chime's acquisition of a sponsor bank validates the balance-sheet model SoFi established four years ago to lower wholesale funding costs. However, a sharp contraction in software revenue and a resilient rate environment leave the stock anchored to a standard bank multiple.
bodyHtml:
In September, Chime agreed to hand over $590 million in cash to acquire Stride Bank. For seven years, the neobank had rented Stride’s balance sheet to process consumer payments and issue debit cards, paying steep sponsor fees for the privilege. Buying the bank outright eliminates that toll booth and permanently lowers its funding costs. In one stroke, Chime placed an explicit market price on the structural advantage SoFi engineered four years ago. Most fintechs are software tenants leasing someone else’s regulatory plumbing; SoFi bought the building.

Strip away the slick mobile interface on your phone, and SoFi Technologies is a consumer bank that people still mistake for an app. It launched in 2011 refinancing student debt for early-career professionals. Today, it operates a nationally chartered bank regulated by the OCC, serving 17.1 million members across personal loans, checking accounts, credit cards, and investment tools. Roughly half of all new products are opened by existing members who arrived for a personal loan and stayed for checking-account direct deposits.

That national bank charter is the company's entire economic engine. When a non-bank fintech issues a loan, it borrows capital from Wall Street warehouse facilities at elevated wholesale rates. SoFi bypasses that middleman by funding its $45.98 billion loan book with $51.3 billion of member deposits. In the September quarter, SoFi paid an average rate of 3.07% on deposits compared to the 4.52% it would pay on warehouse lines. That 145-basis-point spread saved the company roughly $745 million in annualized interest expense and pushed its net interest margin up to 6.14%.

Here is the catch: that funding moat was engineered for an economic cycle where interest rates fall, and that backdrop just changed. October PCE inflation accelerated to 3.8%, third-quarter GDP growth was revised up to 4.3%, and markets now fully price a quarter-point rate hike at the Federal Reserve's December meeting. Meanwhile, SoFi’s new tokenized deposit product, SoFi Earn, yields 4.40% APY to lure capital. At the margin, SoFi is buying deposits at elevated costs rather than harvesting them passively. SoFi's edge is not that it funds cheaper than JPMorgan; it is that it funds cheaper than its former self.

That reality check explains why Wall Street refuses to award the stock a platform valuation. Shares sit roughly 56% below their late-2025 high, trading at about 1.8 times tangible book value and roughly 15 times 2027 earnings guidance. That is a bank multiple for a company growing net revenue 44% year-over-year to $1.385 billion. For the equity to re-rate, the capital-light software business needs to outgrow balance-sheet lending.

Instead, Technology Platform revenue slid 24% to $87.4 million, with contribution margins collapsing from 28% to 16%. SoFi is right to note that a single large client left the platform before the end of 2025, and that revenue grew 18% without it. But contribution profit still fell 56%, which tells you the client that walked was the profitable kind. When lending surges 66% while the software arm shrinks, the market values SoFi as a consumer lender because balance-sheet risk dictates the business.

Short sellers argue that SoFi is an aggressive lender masking deteriorating credit through portfolio sales. While the headline personal loan net charge-off rate declined to 2.26%, that figure is flattered by sales of late-stage delinquent loans. The company’s own all-in estimate of charge-offs sits near 3.4% when factoring in those transactions. Personal loans sit on the balance sheet at fair value rather than amortized cost. So emerging credit losses appear as valuation marks rather than direct provisions, keeping loan loss provisions at just $14.7 million against $52.0 billion in average loans. If the all-in charge-off rate climbs higher while the headline rate remains pinned near 2.3%, the bear thesis confirms that underwriting quality was manufactured through loan sales rather than superior risk modeling.

The business also faces political friction from proposed interest rate caps on consumer credit cards, an intervention that could quickly spread to SoFi’s 12.78% average personal loan coupon. What we are watching next is the Federal Reserve's December 8–9 policy meeting and whether elevated rate expectations compress that 145-basis-point deposit edge. A bank charter frees a fintech from renting capital, but it permanently binds the equity to the risks of managing a balance sheet.

Disclosure: The Signal holds no position in SOFI. Positions may change. This is not financial advice.
